newsitem.title: CHINA: China debt market strides boost rating agency role.
newsitem.headline: China debt market strides boost rating agency role.

text.p: China's growing appetite for corporate debt and its increasing concern with assessing risk are giving a boost to its fledgling credit rating business, officials said on Thursday.

While China Cheng Xin Securities Rating Co Ltd may not have the clout of big rating agencies such as Moody's Investors Service or Standard and Poor's Corp, the leading domestic rating company sees a rising demand for its services.
"We see a growing trend for the issuance of corporate debt," Li Xinhong, Cheng Xin's general manager, told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
"The People's Bank of China (central bank) has made it clear it would like to see this market expanded," he said. "And where you have a real debt market you have a need for rating services."
Cheng Xin rates most debt issued by central government companies and is moving to expand its role in debt offerings by firms under the supervision of regional governments, Li said.

China has been trying to create a financial system based on free market principles and shed the vestiges of a Stalinist centrally planned economy in which any company could expect credit regardless of its ability to repay.
At the same time, Beijing's financial regulators have sought to limit risk, thereby creating even greater demand for tools to help investors to assess risk.
"The market needs information and we are providing that service," Li said. "We are a reference guide for investors."
Li estimated China's corporate debt market would reach 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) this year compared with about 25 billion yuan last year.

In theory, a public debt offer in China must have a rating, but some companies manage to sidestep the regulation by issuing debt to their own employees. Occasionally, such "internal debt" finds its way into public hands.

Cheng Xin was set up in 1992, using the big international rating firms as its role model. It now has about 100 employees and rates long and short term debt as well as providing credit ratings of securities houses and trust companies.
Among Cheng Xin's ratings have been a 3.5 billion yuan Railway Ministry offering and a 1.0 billion Power Ministry offering. Both won the agency's top designation of AAA.
Other companies have not been so fortunate.
"The lowest rating we have given out has been BB," said Li, adding that in some cases, companies unhappy with their rating have scrapped plans for a public offering.
For the time being, Cheng Xin does not make unsolicited ratings.
Most of China's corporate debt is for three years, although the Railway Ministry offer had one five-year tranche.

Corporate debt also cannot pay interest of more than 140 percent of interest on a bank deposit of a similar maturity. A three-year bank deposit pays about eight percent interest and that caps interest on three-year corporate debt at slightly more than 11 percent.
China is also trying to build up an interbank repurchasing market for treasury debt as a way to strengthen its financial sector. This eventually could help the corporate debt market.
"We don't rate treasury debt offers," said Li. "But this will contribute to the creation of a mature financial market, and that will benefit us."
China has also opened its financial sector to competition and a number of new banks have sprung up around the country in recent years.
Li said many investors would want to know the credit position of these new financial institutions. "In the coming years we expect to be rating these banks."
